after.title: Preprint: Clinical outcomes of bio-interventional cyclodialysis with one or multiple allogeneic reinforcements: a multicenter real-world evidence study
after.authors: Chaya, C.; Radcliffe, N. M.; Qiu, M.; Sieminski, S.; Patel, S.; Ianchulev, T.; Ferreira, G.; Shah, M.; Bacharach, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: New York Eye and Ear of Mount Sinai
after.abstract: Introduction: Bio-reinforced cyclodialysis uses an acellular scleral allograft spacer to maintain a surgically created cleft and enhance uveoscleral outflow. Surgeons may place one spacer or two, but whether the second adds IOP lowering has not been reported. We tested whether two spacers achieve greater 12-month IOP reduction than one, and whether any difference persists after adjustment for measured baseline differences. Methods: Observational analysis of 310 eyes in the prospective, multicenter CREST study undergoing combined phacoemulsification and bio-reinforced cyclodialysis with one spacer (n = 170) or two (n = 140). The primary endpoint was IOP change from baseline to month 12. Analyses comprised unadjusted comparison, baseline-adjusted regression, 1:1 propensity-score matching, doubly robust overlap weighting, and models accounting for enrolling site. IOP after a secondary IOP-lowering procedure was censored. Results: At baseline, IOP was 17.9 (4.4) versus 18.7 (5.8) mmHg and medications 1.19 (1.11) versus 1.46 (1.35), with one versus two spacers. The largest imbalance was enrolling site: one center contributed 43.6% of two-spacer eyes but 7.1% of one-spacer eyes. The unadjusted difference in IOP reduction was 2.52 mmHg (95% CI 1.20, 3.84; p<0.001), and persisted after propensity-score matching (2.36 mmHg; 0.94, 3.77; p=0.001) and overlap weighting (1.99 mmHg; 1.18, 2.79; p<0.001). After accounting for site it attenuated to 0.86 mmHg (-0.10 to 1.81; p=0.080), and to 0.42 mmHg (-0.61 to 1.45; p=0.42) within sites using both strategies. Medication reduction (-0.69 versus -0.62; p=0.64) and secondary IOP-lowering procedures (2.9% versus 2.9%; p=1.0) did not differ. Conclusion: Two-spacer treatment was associated with greater 12-month IOP reduction in unadjusted and patient-level adjusted analyses, but this association was substantially attenuated after accounting for enrolling site. These real-world data are compatible with, but do not establish, an independent incremental effect of a second spacer. A randomized comparison is required to determine whether spacer number independently influences IOP reduction.

after.title: Preprint: Robust Feature Engineering Techniques for Designing Efficient Motor Imagery-Based Systems Using Multidomain Electroencephalography
after.authors: Ahmed, S. S.; Jawed, S.; Khan, M. A.; Fazal, Z. Z.; Shehryar, T.; Bukhari, S. M.; Khan, R. A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Medical College, Aga Khan University, Karachi, Pakistan; Byers Eye Institute, Stanford University School of Medicine, Palo Alto, United States
after.abstract: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have potential applications in neurorehabilitation; however, the high dimensionality and complexity of electroencephalography (EEG) signals present challenges for accurate classification. This study aimed to improve the classification of motor and motor imagery activities using multidomain feature engineering and feature selection on the MILimbEEG dataset. Time-domain, frequency-domain, and wavelet-based features were extracted from 16-channel EEG signals, yielding 416 features. Maximum relevance minimum redundancy (MRMR) was then applied to select the four most informative and minimally redundant features. These features were used to train support vector machine (SVM), K-nearest neighbors (KNN), Naive Bayes, and decision tree classifiers, with performance evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation based on testing accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The Gaussian-kernel SVM achieved the highest testing accuracies of 92.50% for motor activities and 95.48% for motor imagery activities. For the highest-performing motor imagery classification, precision, recall, and F1-score were 86.97%, 88.33%, and 87.04%, respectively. These findings demonstrate that reducing 416 multidomain EEG features to four discriminative features using MRMR can maintain strong classification performance. The proposed feature-engineering framework may support the development of computationally efficient EEG-based BCI systems for neurorehabilitation applications.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Histological characteristics of the quadriceps muscle and their associations with gait in older adults

after.title: Preprint: Histological characteristics of the quadriceps muscle and their associations with gait in older adults
after.authors: Oveisgharan, S.; Longo, S.; Yang, J.; Schneider, J. A.; Bennett, D. A.; Delbono, O.; Buchman, A. S.
after.abstract: Background/objective: There is a paucity of data about muscle morphology in aging adults. We quantified histologic features of the quadriceps muscle and examined their associations with gait function and physical activity in community-dwelling older adults. Methods: Participants were from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Postmortem sections of the quadriceps muscles were examined by immunohistochemistry using antibodies against myosin heavy chain, and histological characteristics of the quadriceps muscles were derived through images quantifications and segmentations. In addition, brain sections were assessed for collection of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias pathologies. Before death, participants' physical activity was objectively measured through wearing an accelerometer sensor for 10 days, and gait function was quantified by walking 8 feet and turning 360o twice. Linear regressions and compositional analyses were used for analyzing data. Results: Postmortem quadriceps was examined in 236 decedents (mean age at death was 91.7 years (SD=6.0), and 71.6% (n=169) were females. On average, 44.7% (SD=19.5) of the muscle fibers were type I and 54.2% (SD=19.4) were type II, and 40.6% (SD=13.0) and 21.9% (12.9) of the quadriceps muscle area were composed of type I and II muscle fibers, respectively. In compositional analyses, male sex (estimate=0.303, SE=0.126, p=0.016) and more physical activity (estimate=0.118, SE=0.059, p=0.045) were associated with larger quadriceps muscle areas with type II muscle fibers, which were related to better gait (estimate=-0.049, SE=0.021, p=0.021). Quadriceps muscle composition explained an additional 3.2% of gait's variance beyond the 5.8% variance explained by Alzheimer's disease and related dementias brain pathologies. Conclusion: Quadriceps muscles having larger areas with type II muscle fibers were associated with more physical activity and better gait function in aging adults. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying these associations are critical for developing new therapies.

after.title: Preprint: Trait-Level Rather Than Individual-Level Resolution in Fitness Genomics: A Population-Calibrated Variant Prioritization Framework in a South Asian Cohort
after.authors: UPPALURI, K. R.; Challa, H. J.; Vempati, K. K.; Kadali, L. N.; Rayala, M. B. V.; Malluri, B.; Jayanthy, P.
after.abstract: Translating candidate gene panels into objective physiological trait interpretations remains a major hurdle in exercise genomics. Conventional total genotype scoring suffers from severe panel-composition bias, fails to evaluate unannotated or novel variants, and frequently fosters inflated claims regarding individual athletic prediction. Here, we present a population-calibrated, multi-tiered computational framework that evaluates genomic variation across six evidence streams integrating deep learning protein and genomic language models (ESM-2, Evo 2), missense and splice predictors (AlphaMissense, SpliceAI), and regional pathogenic-density metrics to generate a continuous Variant Priority Score (VPS; 1-10 scale). By dynamically renormalizing missing evidence streams rather than zero-filling them, the framework robustly scores unannotated variants lacking empirical database entries. Individual trait burden across 344 genes (spanning 17 physiological traits in Aerobic, Anaerobic, and Recovery domains) is aggregated and normalized against ancestry-matched expectations derived from gnomAD South Asian and an in-house reference cohort (N > 13,000). When applied to 960 South Indian individuals (584 male, 376 female; whole-exome sequencing), this normalization removed the dependence of expected trait burden on panel size by construction, and gene count explained only 2.7% of the variance in the resulting capacity scores (six traits interrogated by 16 to 33 genes). Variance partitioning of 4,764 individual-by-trait scores (six of the 17 traits: one aerobic, two anaerobic and three recovery) revealed that score variation was predominantly trait-driven (45.5%) rather than individual-driven (11.1%, p = 0.386), a pattern reproduced independently in males and females and with no statistically significant gender difference in capacity scores, indicating that, in this cohort, the candidate panel resolved differences between physiological traits but did not detect differences between individuals in capacity scores (no athletic phenotype was measured). Benchmarking against ClinVar classifications achieved an AUC of 0.74, which fell to 0.62 when archive-dependent streams were excluded, directly quantifying the role of shared data provenance. Replacing the in-house frequency reference with gnomAD South Asian shifted absolute scores (median fold change 0.73) but preserved trait ordering (Spearman 0.96), so scores are positions against a stated, population-specific reference. This framework provides an auditable, evidence-traceable baseline for trait-level research and functional variant prioritization while offering a critical methodological safeguard against over-interpreting unvalidated individual performance predictions.

after.title: Preprint: Gut microbiome and incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events in the general population: a prospective study in five European cohorts
after.authors: Kambur, O.; Grahnemo, L.; Nethander, M.; Pertiwi, K.; Dekkers, K.; Smith, J. G.; Engström, G.; Ärnlöv, J.; Orho-Melander, M.; Kullberg, R. F. J.; Haak, B. W.; Galenkamp, H.; van den Born, B.-J. H.; Nieuwdorp, M.; Koponen, K.; Meric, G.; Knight, R.; Niiranen, T. J.; Hveem, K.; Fall, T.; Larsson, S. C.; Ohlsson, C.; Salomaa, V.; Havulinna, A. S.
after.abstract: Background: Accumulating evidence suggests that the gut microbiota is implicated in cardiovascular disease. We investigated how the gut microbiome associates with incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and cardiovascular and all-cause mortality (ACM) in a large, prospective, population-based study. The findings were tested for replication in four independent cohorts. Methods: Gut microbiome composition was assessed via shallow shotgun sequencing in the FINRISK 2002 cohort, with up to 18 years of follow-up. Associations of microbial taxa with incident MACE were investigated using time-to-event analyses. Significant associated microbial features were tested for replication in four European cohorts (HUNT, HELIUS, SIMPLER, and SCAPIS) followed by a meta-analysis. Results: In the FINRISK 2002 cohort (1167 incident MACE events), nine taxa were significantly associated with incident MACE and sustained adjustments for traditional risk factors and multiple comparisons. The meta-analysis of replication cohorts (N=30,228; 1,938 participants with incident MACE) confirmed robust associations for several identified taxa. Specifically, higher abundance of genera Scardovia (HR=1.17 [95% CI 1.08-1.26], p= 0.0001) and Limosilactobacillus (HR=1.16 [95%CI 1.09-1.23], p= 1E-06) was associated with increased MACE risk, and increased risk of cardiovascular mortality and all-cause mortality. The species ER4 sp900317525 (HR=0.89 [95%CI 0.83-0.95], p=0.0005) was associated with lower hazard of MACE and all-cause mortality. Conclusions: The gut metagenome showed robust associations with incident MACE, which were replicated in four independent European cohorts. Key microbial taxa also associated with incident MACE and mortality, suggesting their potential relevance as candidate risk markers for further studies.

after.title: Preprint: DermNet: An Incremental Knowledge Distillation Framework for Accurate and Robust Skin Layer Segmentation
after.authors: Abdul Salam, A.; Akram, M. U.; Jawed, S.; Shehryar, T.; Fazal, Z. Z.; Yousaf, M. H.; Rao, B.; Alghamdi, N. S.
after.abstract: Background Accurate segmentation of skin layers in histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs) is important for identifying disease-associated structural changes and supporting computer-aided dermatopathological analysis. However, existing approaches are often restricted to single magnification levels and may inadequately capture the heterogeneous morphological characteristics of individual skin layers. We propose DermNet, a multi-resolution class-incremental learning framework designed to achieve accurate skin layer segmentation while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Methods DermNet employs a SegFormer backbone within a teacher-student architecture and progressively learns class-specific features from WSIs acquired at 10x, 5x, and 2x magnifications. The framework incorporates exemplar replay, mutual knowledge, distillation, classification, Kullback-Leibler divergence losses, boundary loss, and Elastic Weight Consolidation to preserve previously learned representations while incorporating new tissue classes. The model was trained and evaluated using a publicly available dataset of 290 WSIs, with segmentation focused on the epidermis, papillary dermis, reticular dermis, hypodermis, keratin, and background. Results DermNet consistently outperformed U-Net and alternative SegFormer training strategies across all three magnification levels. At 10x magnification, DermNet achieved Dice scores of 0.95 for epidermis, 0.92 for papillary dermis, 0.94 for reticular dermis, 0.97 for keratin, and 0.98 for hypodermis, outperforming UNet++ and DeepLabv3+. TransUNet, SwinUNet, and nnU-Net under the same experimental conditions. Evaluation on an independent publicly available dataset further demonstrated cross-dataset generalizability, with Dice scores ranging from 0.89 to 0.97 across classes. Conclusion DermNet enables accurate and robust multi-resolution skin layer segmentation by combining class-incremental learning with knowledge distillation and mechanisms for preserving previously learned features. Its performance across magnification levels and an independent dataset supports its potential for scalable and generalizable automated dermatopathological image analysis.

after.title: Preprint: Associations between different intensities of leisure-time physical activity and subsequent psychotropic medication use among young and early midlife adults: a register-linked follow-up study
after.authors: Jarvensivu, L.; Paivarinne, V.; Rahkonen, O.; Lallukka, T.
after.abstract: Introduction Previous studies have not examined associations between physical activity intensity and subsequent psychotropic medication use. We examined associations between different leisure-time physical activity (LTPA) intensities and subsequent psychotropic medication purchases. Methods We used Helsinki Health Study questionnaire data collected in 2017 from 19-39-year-old employees of the City of Helsinki, linked to register data on psychotropic medication purchases from 2014 to 2022 (82.5% consented to the register linkage). The analytical sample included 4,160 participants (80.4% women, representing the target population). Weekly hours of light (LPA), moderate (MPA) and vigorous (VPA) LTPA were examined separately. Cox proportional hazards regression with restricted cubic splines was used to examine nonlinear associations with the first psychotropic medication purchase during follow-up, adjusting for prior medication and sociodemographic and health-related covariates. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. Results During the follow-up, 28.1% of participants had at least one psychotropic medication purchase. After adjustment for age and gender, VPA was associated with psychotropic medication purchases (overall p<0.001; nonlinearity p<0.001), whereas MPA and LPA were not. Further adjustments and stratification by prior psychotropic medication purchase status attenuated the VPA association (overall p=0.0041). In this model, for 5 versus 0 hours/week of VPA, the HR was 0.79 (95% CI 0.68-0.91), corresponding to approximately 23 fewer first-purchase events per 1,000 participants over three years. Conclusions Higher-intensity LTPA appeared more strongly associated with a lower hazard of psychotropic medication purchases, although only the VPA association saw clear support.

after.authors: Ashfaque, M.; Ghani, U.; Bhagwat, S.; Farmer, S. F.; Niazi, I. K.; Pujari, A. N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Neu(RAL)2: NeuRAL Systems and Rehabilitation and Assistive Technologies Laboratory, School of Physics, Engineering and Computer Science, University of Hertfords
after.abstract: Cutaneous sensation is vital for daily function and safety, yet it commonly declines with ageing and after neurological injury, with stroke survivors particularly affected. This study investigates whether sub-threshold stochastic (random) vibrations can enhance light-touch (cutaneous) sensation in healthy adults and stroke survivors and characterizes the associated changes in cortical functional connectivity (FC). Nineteen healthy participants and five stroke survivors took part. A custom device delivered sinusoidal and stochastic vibrations to the volar surface of the right middle fingertip. For each participant we first determined the detection threshold for stochastic vibration alone, then the threshold for a 30 Hz sinusoidal vibration, and then the threshold for that sinusoidal vibration combined with imperceptible stochastic noise fixed at 80% of the stochastic threshold; in ten healthy participants a super-threshold combination (120% of the stochastic threshold) was also tested. High-density (64-channel) electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded throughout for the healthy participants. Adding sub- threshold stochastic noise lowered the sinusoidal detection threshold in every participant tested and produced consistent reductions in all five stroke survivors; expressed as gains in sensitivity, individual improvements reached up to 19 times in healthy participants and up to 4 times in stroke survivors. Source- localized EEG showed that sub-threshold stochastic vibration significantly increased FC, most extensively in the alpha band, with prominent involvement of frontal regions (superior and rostral middle frontal cortices and anterior cingulate; cluster- based permutation p < 0.05), consistent with a noise-driven modulation of sensory and attentional networks. Super-threshold noise produced weaker, predominantly beta-band changes, in line with signal masking rather than resonance. These findings indicate that sub-threshold stochastic vibration lowers light-touch detection thresholds and reorganizes cortical connectivity in both healthy and stroke populations, and they support prioritizing cutaneous sensation in stochastic-resonance based neurorehabilitation for stroke survivors.

after.title: Preprint: A Multi-Cohort nnU-Net for White Matter Hyperintensity Segmentation Across 2D and 3D FLAIR Acquisitions
after.authors: Chen, Y.; Khatri, U.; Xu, B.; Astafiev, S. V.; Ford, A.; Lee, J.-M.; An, H.; Phuah, C.-L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Barrow Neuro Analytics Center, Barrow Neurological Institute, Phoenix, AZ; Departments of Neurology and Neurosurgery, Barrow Neurological Institute, Phoenix, AZ
after.abstract: Background White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are increasingly pooled across aging, cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), and dementia cohorts that differ in both disease composition and FLAIR acquisition. Most automated segmentation tools were developed within a narrower range of populations or protocols, and few have been tested for whether segmentation accuracy and error remain consistent across conventional 2D and isotropic 3D FLAIR, or whether the choice of algorithm alters downstream clinical associations. Methods We developed a single nnU-Net model, taking FLAIR and T1-weighted images as inputs, using 460 2D and 3D FLAIR scans from a neurodegenerative cohort (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, ADNI), a CSVD-enriched cohort with same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR (Washington University White Matter Ischemic-Hypoxia study, WWISH), and a population-based sample (UK Biobank), holding out 92 scans from 66 participants at the participant-level as an internal test set. We further evaluated the model in an independent ADNI3 3D FLAIR set (n = 25), benchmarking voxel-wise overlap (Dice), volumetric agreement, and lesion-level detection against SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and FreeSurfer WMH-SynthSeg, and compared acquisition-specific volume bias in participants with paired 2D and 3D FLAIR. We then compared how WMH volumes from each method predicted incident dementia in cognitively unimpaired adults from ADNI and the Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (n = 1,174; 42 incident cases). Results In the internal test set, the model achieved a mean Dice of 0.73 (SD 0.10), compared with 0.50, 0.57, and 0.29 for SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and WMH-SynthSeg (all FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). Dice was similar on 2D and 3D FLAIR (0.75 vs. 0.71). In WWISH participants imaged with both acquisitions, mean volume bias differed between 2D and 3D scans by 1.8 mL for the model versus 4.7-9.9 mL for the comparators. Advantages were largest in low-burden scans (<5 mL; Dice 0.66 vs. 0.19-0.54) and for lesions of [≤]100 voxels (detection 77-87% vs. 14-63%). In ADNI3, the model retained a mean Dice of 0.70 (SD 0.14) without retraining and exceeded all comparators (FDR-adjusted p [≤] 0.002). Model-derived WMH volume was associated with incident dementia beyond clinical covariates (OR per SD 1.40, 95% CI 1.11-1.77; likelihood-ratio p = 0.009; cross-validated AUC 0.71 vs. 0.68), whereas comparator-derived volumes did not significantly improve model fit. Conclusions Training a single model across disease contexts and FLAIR acquisitions yielded WMH segmentation that was similarly accurate on 2D and 3D FLAIR, sensitive to low-burden disease, transferable to an unseen protocol, and clinically informative, supporting its use in multi-cohort, mixed-etiology studies.

after.title: Preprint: Bacteriological Contamination of Shared Bicycle Handlebars and Hand Hygiene Practices of Users at Makerere University, Kampala, Uganda.
after.authors: TENDO, C. D.; Muleme, J.; Halage, A. A.; Mwaka, R. N.; Nabagala, C.; Walusimbi, M.; Ssemugabo, C.
after.abstract: Background Bacteriological surface contamination is a key pathway for pathogen transmission, with potential implications for microbial exposure. Shared bicycles at Makerere University provide sustainable transport, but frequent handling of handlebars may facilitate colonization and spread of bacteria such as E. coli. This study aimed to identify prevalent bacterial species on shared bicycle handlebars, their microbial load and antimicrobial profiles, and users' hand hygiene practices influencing contamination at Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda. Methods We randomly sampled 100 shared bicycles and interviewed their respective users. Handlebar swabs were cultured and analyzed by culture-based enumeration. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using disk diffusion across six antibiotics. Hand hygiene data were collected using structured questionnaire guides. Descriptive statistics summarized bacterial counts, F-tests assessed statistical differences within and across bacterial species, and modified poisson regression examined associations between hygiene practices and contamination. Results Contamination was detected on 56% (56/100) of the sampled handlebars. From the 56 contaminated samples, 13 contained more than one bacterial species and 75 isolates were recovered, with S. aureus at 68% (51/75) as the most prevalent isolate. Microbial loads differed significantly across species (F (2, 63) = 12.78, p < 0.0001). 35 of the 75 isolates yielded bacteriological growth and were subjected to AST. Most isolates were resistant to erythromycin at 71% (25/35), and S. aureus showed resistance to five of six antibiotics, indicating multidrug resistance. Users who did not clean their hands were (APR = 1.61, 95% CI: 1.11-1.98) 1.6 times more likely to contaminate handlebars. Conclusion Shared bicycle handlebars at Makerere University were contaminated with potentially pathogenic bacteria, indicating a potential hygiene concern. Not cleaning hands was associated with contamination of bicycle handlebars. The service provider urgently needs to promote proper hand hygiene by installing hand-washing stations with soap or sanitizers at docking points

after.title: Preprint: Detecting Contradictory Evidence on Drug-Disease Associations at Scale
after.authors: Lan, M.; Menke, J.; Liu, S.; Lu, Z.; Kilicoglu, H.
after.abstract: Contradictory claims about drug efficacy across randomized controlled trials (RCTs) complicate evidence-based medicine, yet existing automated methods classify isolated sentence pairs and do not explain why studies disagree. We present DrugCon, a large language model (LLM)-based framework that extracts study conclusions from RCT abstracts, links these claims when they concern the same drug-disease association, detects contradictions with counterfactual reasoning, and explains them using a taxonomy of ten study-level factors such as population, dosage, and outcome measures. Applying DrugCon to 224,756 RCT abstracts, we built DrugCon-Bench, an exhaustively annotated benchmark of 542 contradictory claim pairs from 819 abstracts. Most contradictions involve more than one study-level factor (75.5%). The most common are differences in outcome measures (64.0%), populations (51.3%), and dosage or exposure duration (35.6%). DrugCon achieves an F1 score of 0.744 for contradiction detection, outperforming rule-based, supervised, and natural language inference baselines, and an F1 of 0.482 for identifying explanatory study factors. DrugCon enables scalable and explainable analysis of contradictory clinical evidence.

after.title: Preprint: Assessment of Undergraduate Psychological Wellbeing Using Explainable Machine Learning: A Study from Sri Lanka
after.authors: Paranawithana, G.; Perera, A.; Kumburegama, S.; Seelagama, P.; Hettigoda, K.; Kamalrathne, T.; Bulathwatta, A.; Herath, D.; Perera, S.; Fernando, B.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Peradeniya Faculty of Veterinary Medicine and Animal Science
after.abstract: Academic, psychosocial, financial, environmental, and interpersonal factors are widely recognized as important contributors to the overall wellbeing of students. This study aimed to identify factors associated with the psychological wellbeing of university undergraduates and compare the performance of machine learning models for binary and multiclass classification of wellbeing status using self-reported survey data from undergraduates at the University of Peradeniya, Sri Lanka. The findings may facilitate the early identification of students with lower wellbeing and inform targeted interventions to foster a healthier and more supportive academic environment. Cross-sectional questionnaire data from 2,913 undergraduates were analyzed to classify psychological wellbeing using overall happiness scores. Scores were grouped into binary (1-5 and 6-9) and multiclass (1-4, 5-6, and 7-9) categories. Data preprocessing included missing value imputation, one-hot encoding, and feature scaling where appropriate. Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), XGBoost (XGB), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) models were trained using repeated stratified 10-fold cross-validation and evaluated using macro F1-score, ROC-AUC, and classification reports. SHAP analysis was employed to interpret feature contributions and enhance model interpretability. XGB achieved the highest macro-F1 score (70.5%) for binary classification, with a test accuracy of 72.5%. The model correctly classified 63.6% and 80% of participants in the lower and higher psychological wellbeing groups, respectively. For multiclass classification, RF achieved the highest macro-F1 score (54.6%), with a test accuracy of 56.5%. The model correctly classified 48%, 57%, and 60% of participants in the lower, intermediate, and higher psychological wellbeing groups, respectively. SHAP analysis identified academic coping, health and wellbeing, financial circumstances, and interpersonal relationships as key predictors of psychological wellbeing across both models. These findings demonstrate the potential of machine learning to classify psychological wellbeing groups using self-reported data, supporting early identification of students at risk of poor wellbeing and informing targeted university-level mental health interventions.

after.title: Preprint: MENTOR: An Evidence-Informed Large Language Model-Based Multi-Agent System for Efficient Selection of Institution-Specific Negative Control Outcomes
after.authors: Yang, T.; Chang, J.; Kim, Y.; Cho, J.; Choi, K.; Son, M.; Kim, C.
after.abstract: Objective Negative control outcomes (NCOs) help detect and correct systematic error in observational studies, yet their selection remains largely manual. The Common Evidence Model (CEM) can generate candidate lists, but researchers must still screen them for plausibility as true nulls and for sufficient observation in each institution's data. We developed and evaluated MENTOR (Multi-agent Evidence-informed Negative conTrol Outcome selection with Reasoning), a multi-agent system of large language models (LLMs) that combines CEM evidence with LLM reasoning to select institution-specific NCOs. Methods Four LLM agents operate on an institution's Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership common data model. A Curator summarizes drug labels, a Suggester assesses locally frequent candidates with CEM evidence and a first-pass LLM judgment, an Adjudicator resolves their disagreements, and a Diagnostician relaxes the patient-count threshold until a target number of NCOs is met. Using Qwen3.6-27B, we evaluated 349 candidates for three drug pairs in a Korean tertiary hospital's electronic health records (2.9 million patients) against a blinded LLM judge from a different model family, validated by three experts on 90 candidates. We compared accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), and sensitivity with CEM-only and first-pass-LLM-only selection. Results MENTOR proposed 243 NCOs versus 121 by CEM-only, with higher accuracy (0.83 [0.79-0.87] vs. 0.53 [0.48-0.58]), sensitivity (0.89 vs. 0.41), and PPV (0.86 vs. 0.79). Judge-expert agreement was {kappa}=0.63. Adjudication, needed for 44.1% of candidates, added little accuracy, and only with reasoning mode. Concordant acceptances, which bypass it, contained about half of the false positives. Only 7%-9% of CEM-proposed outcomes had at least 10,000 patients at the institution. Conclusion Combining LLM judgments with CEM evidence and local data yielded more NCOs, with higher PPV, than CEM alone. Restricting reasoning to discordant candidates kept computation time below 40% of that with reasoning in all agents. Every decision comes with its evidence and rationale for investigators' final review.

after.title: Preprint: Multilevel Interventions to Improve Colonoscopy Completion After Abnormal Fecal Immunochemical Testing in a Safety-Net Health System: Preliminary Findings from the IMPACTT Study
after.authors: Sarkar, U.; Wong, J.; Olazo, K.; Colom Brana, S.; Patel, S.; Pasick, R.; McCulloch, C.; Somsouk, M.
after.abstract: Background: Timely diagnostic colonoscopy is a critical step after an abnormal fecal immunochemical test (FIT), yet many patients do not complete follow-up within recommended timeframes, particularly in safety-net settings. Barriers occur across multiple levels and stages of care, suggesting a need for interventions that address both clinic processes and patient-level barriers. Methods: IMProving Adherence to Colonoscopy through Teams and Technology (IMPACTT) evaluated two concurrent interventions across 12 adult primary care clinics in the San Francisco Health Network. A clinic-level Best Practice Bundle (BPB), implemented in a stepped-wedge rollout, included patient tracking, standardized electronic health record documentation, standardized education and communication, and audit and feedback. In parallel, we randomly assigned eligible patients to a patient-level instruction and navigation (PIN) intervention or usual care. PIN provided targeted outreach to patients who were neither referred nor scheduled, as well as multilingual text reminders that allowed patients to confirm, cancel, or reschedule their colonoscopy. The primary outcome was colonoscopy completion within 180 days of an abnormal FIT. This preliminary analysis reports unadjusted comparisons among patients with sufficient follow-up at the data cutoff. Results: Among 2,303 patients with an abnormal FIT, 1,136 were identified before and 1,167 after their clinic implemented the BPB. Colonoscopy completion within 180 days was 44.1% before BPB implementation and 60.1% after implementation (risk difference, 16.0 percentage points; 95% CI, 11.8 to 20.1; p<0.001). Referral to gastroenterology within 42 days increased from 69.8% to 84.2%, and among patients who completed colonoscopy, the median time from FIT to colonoscopy decreased from 131 to 86 days. In the randomized PIN trial, we assigned 1,415 patients to usual care (n=698) or PIN (n=717). Colonoscopy completion within 180 days did not differ between usual care and PIN (58.4% vs 57.7%; risk difference, -0.7 percentage points; 95% CI, -5.9 to 4.6; p=0.9). PIN also did not improve referral within 42 days or scheduling within 56 days. Conclusions: In preliminary unadjusted analyses, implementation of a clinic-level bundle targeting tracking, communication, documentation, and feedback was associated with improved timely follow-up after abnormal FIT, whereas a randomized technology-supported patient instruction and navigation intervention did not improve colonoscopy completion. Prespecified analyses accounting for calendar time, clinic-level clustering, patient characteristics, and concurrent intervention assignment are forthcoming. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06191185.

after.title: Preprint: Its the Art of Listening": Patient and Practitioner Perspectives on Acute Cardiac Care for Patients with a Severe Mental Illness (SMI): A Qualitative Interview Study
after.authors: Vettini, A.; Cavers, D.; Mercer, S.; Jackson, C.; Fleetwood, K.; Padmanabhan, S.; Smith, D.
after.abstract: Background: Patients with a severe mental illness experience disparities in acute cardiac care, yet reasons underlying these inequities remain poorly understood. We aimed to explore patient and healthcare professional perspectives of acute cardiac care to identify factors influencing care quality and equity. Methods and results: We conducted semi-structured videocall interviews with people with a severe mental illness who had been hospitalised following a myocardial infarction, and with Cardiology and Emergency Room healthcare professionals involved in acute cardiac care across two central Scottish health boards between July 2023 and April 2024. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis in NVivo. We conducted 21 interviews (13 healthcare professionals; 8 people with a severe mental illness). Although many patients reported empathic and supportive care, barriers were described. We identified 3 themes from the data: positive care experiences; cross-cutting care barriers, and challenges along the care pathway. Healthcare professionals sought to provide equitable care but reported challenges related to limited mental health training, diagnostic uncertainty, behavioural management and difficulties accessing psychiatric expertise, prescribed medication and associated information. Patients described experiences of stigma, communication difficulties, disruptions to psychiatric medication continuity and distress associated with overstimulating hospital environments. System-level barriers included staff shortages, limited access to liaison psychiatry, lack of clear care protocols and difficulties integrating mental and physical healthcare. Positive experiences were associated with empathic staff, feeling listened to, clear communication, and tailored efforts to create psychologically safe care environments. Conclusion: Inequities in acute cardiac care for people with a severe mental illness appear to arise from the interaction of patient complexity, clinician uncertainty and organisational constraints. Improving care will require greater integration of mental and physical health services, continuity of psychiatric treatment, psychologically-informed care environments, and support for staff delivering care to this complex patient group.

after.title: Preprint: An observational study examining nasopharyngeal resistome evolution among children under the selective pressure of antibiotic exposure and hospitalisation for pneumonia in Malawi: A study protocol
after.authors: O'Connor, L.; Kalizang'oma, A.; Chimalizeni, Y.; Meehan, C.; Androga, G.; Brown, C.; Henrion, M.; Chaguza, C.; French, N.; Heyderman, R. S.; Kwambana-Adams, B.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, UK
after.abstract: Introduction Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) to first line antibiotics for pneumonia is a major global health problem, and AMR-attributable deaths are prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa. Improved data on how AMR develops and influences health outcomes in resource limited settings is crucial. The nasopharynx is a reservoir for pneumonia pathogens and their resistome, the genetic determinants of AMR. No study has explored whether human resistome composition in children with pneumonia is associated with health outcomes. This study will examine whether antibiotic treatment and hospital admission for pneumonia generate a persistent hospital-acquired nasopharyngeal resistome in children, and whether this is associated with re-hospitalisation. Methods This is an observational case-control study, that will recruit 350 children aged 12-36 months from four groups in Blantyre, Malawi: healthy children in the community (healthy community), children with pneumonia treated in the community (community pneumonia), children hospitalised with pneumonia (hospital pneumonia) and children re-hospitalised with pneumonia (re-hospitalised pneumonia). Nasopharyngeal swabs will be taken at recruitment and 3-month follow-up study visits for metagenomic sequencing to characterise the nasopharyngeal microbiome and resistome; urine samples will be taken at recruitment for an antibiotic activity bioassay. Socio-demographic data, co-morbidities, pneumonia severity, antibiotic exposure and health outcomes will be recorded. Analysis Cross-sectional comparisons between groups at recruitment will examine whether nasopharyngeal resistome (NPR) composition differs by pneumonia severity, antibiotic and healthcare exposure. Longitudinal comparisons within groups will assess the dynamics of NPR composition over time. The study is powered to detect a medium effect size (Cohens D = 0.505) change in the relative abundance of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) between all four groups. Primary outcomes are the difference in beta diversity (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity index), and relative abundance of ARG classes in the NPR. The primary objectives are to estimate the difference in diversity and relative abundance of the NPR between hospitalised pneumonia participants when compared to 1) healthy community and 2) community pneumonia participants, and to investigate whether participants re-hospitalised with pneumonia within a 3-month period have a persistent hospital-acquired NPR pattern. Ethics and dissemination The study has been approved by the Kamuzu University of Heath Sciences Research Ethics Committee (KUREC, formerly Malawi College of Medicine Research Ethics Committee; Ref: P.10/24-1200) and Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine Research Ethics Committee (LSTM REC; Ref: 24-076). Trial registration number ISRCTN64027792

after.title: Preprint: Altered herpesvirus-specific immune response is associated with long COVID
after.authors: Joshi, R. V.; Khan, R. M.; Jackson, K. J.; Ballouz, S.; Jacka, B.; Ni, L.; Findell-Aghnatios, N.; Aggarwal, A.; Turville, S. G.; Singh, M.; Kim, K. W.; Yau, C.; Byrne, A.; Brew, B. J.; Dore, G. J.; Darley, D. R.; Matthews, G. V.; Kelleher, A. D.; Phetsouphanh, C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The Kirby Institute, University of New South Wales
after.abstract: Long COVID is associated with persistent immune dysregulation, but whether immunity to latent viruses is also altered remains unclear. We profiled herpesvirus-specific antibodies and T-cell responses in people with long COVID and recovered convalescent controls at 4, 8, and 24 months after SAR-CoV-2 infection. Overall antibody reactivity and abundance against cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) responder frequencies and circulating B-cell subsets were broadly preserved, but early antibody avidity and virus-specific CD4 T cell response magnitude were reduced. Neither virus nucleic acid was detected in plasma or stool at 4 or 8 months. Here, we show that long COVID is associated with selective, time-dependent alteration of herpesvirus-specific immune memory, including relatively preserved or enhanced CD8 responses and greater representation of selected herpesvirus-associated T-cell receptor clonotypes. Together, these findings indicate altered herpesvirus-specific antibody quality despite broadly preserved antibody abundance. Lower EBV avidity was associated with poorer quality of life and unrecovered status.

after.authors: van Dyk, J.; Masini, T.; Lambert, S. M.; Darlong, J.; Deps, P. D.; Nobre, M. L.; van Brakel, W.; Hill, B.; Timalsina, A. B.; Mane, S. S.; Modali, S. A.; Malik, P.; Lal, V.; Wasmann, R. E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Division of Clinical Pharmacology, Department of Medicine, University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa
after.abstract: Background: Dosing guidance for children with leprosy remains operationally challenging. For children under 10 years of age, current WHO recommendations rely on mg/kg dosing of the three separate components of leprosy multidrug therapy, which are difficult to implement in routine care and may result in inconsistent drug exposures. Weight-banded dosing offers a pragmatic alternative that better aligns with pharmacokinetic principles and existing drug formulations. Methodology: A pharmacokinetic simulation study was conducted to develop harmonized weight-banded dosing regimens for rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone in children aged 2 to <10 years. Using the WHO dosing tool, drug exposures across harmonized weight bands were simulated and adult-equivalent systemic exposure (80-125% of adult area under the concentration-time curve) targeted. Predicted exposures were contextualized against safety reference regimens used in tuberculosis meningitis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, and leprosy. An iterative review process involving the WHO Technical Working Group on leprosy in children ensured clinical and operational feasibility. Results: Proposed weight-banded multidrug therapy regimens achieved adult-equivalent exposures across most weight bands. Predicted exposures modestly exceeded 125% of adult levels at the lower end of selected weight bands but remained well below safety benchmarks, namely exposures associated with daily rifampicin therapy for tuberculosis meningitis and clofazimine regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Dapsone exposures were comparable to those achieved with current leprosy dosing. The existing 10-14-year-old child MDT blister pack could be used without modification in children weighing 25-39.9 kg and with limited tablet or gel capsule removal in children weighing 6-24.9 kg. Conclusions: A harmonized weight-banded dosing strategy was developed that enables effective, practical dosing of leprosy multidrug therapy in children under 10 years using existing free-of-charge blister packs provided through WHO. This approach improves dosing consistency, supports programmatic implementation, and provides a rational interim solution while child-friendly formulations are being developed.

after.title: Preprint: Galantamine for routine neuromuscular block reversal and treatment of emergence delirium in children after ENT surgery: a retrospective observational study
after.authors: Neverov, A. A.; Kairysh, E. A.
after.abstract: Background. Emergence delirium is a common complication of general anesthesia in children. Preschool age and ear, nose and throat (ENT) procedures are risk factors [1, 2, 3, 4]. The hypothesis linking delirium to central cholinergic deficiency provides a rationale for studying galantamine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that crosses the blood-brain barrier and is used to reverse neuromuscular blockade. We assessed the association between its routine administration and emergence delirium in children after ENT surgery under sevoflurane anesthesia. Objective. To compare emergence delirium frequency and Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium (PAED) scores after elective ENT surgery with and without routine reversal of neuromuscular blockade with galantamine, and to describe the course of delirium episodes following therapeutic administration. Methods. This retrospective observational study included 207 children aged 2-17 years who underwent elective ENT surgery, predominantly adenoidectomy, tonsillotomy or tonsillectomy, under sevoflurane-based general anesthesia between October 2025 and January 2026. Data were extracted retrospectively from medical records into a study worksheet. PAED scores were checked against clinical descriptions and corrected where discrepancies were identified. The groups reflected the practices of two anesthesiologists. All children in the prophylactic group (n = 102) received galantamine to reverse neuromuscular blockade. In the group without prophylactic administration (n = 105), routine reversal was not performed; galantamine was administered as needed for impaired emergence or suspected residual neuromuscular blockade. The analysis used assessments performed after extubation in the operating room, before treatment for impaired emergence. The primary outcome was PAED > 10, interpreted alongside the clinical descriptions. Results. Prophylactic use. PAED > 10 was recorded in 0 of 102 children receiving routine reversal and 19 of 105 without prophylactic administration (18.1%, p < 0.0001). Median PAED scores were 7 [6-8] and 8 [6-9], respectively (p = 0.0015). Therapeutic use. Intravenous galantamine (2.5-10 mg) was administered in 17 episodes of delirium with motor agitation and impaired interaction. Resolution was documented in all 17 cases. Reduced agitation was accompanied by restoration of meaningful interaction. No sedatives were used to treat delirium. With ondansetron and dexamethasone prophylaxis, emetic events were recorded during the first postoperative hour in 17.6% and 21.9% of children, respectively (p = 0.49). No serious adverse events were documented. Conclusion. No PAED scores > 10 were recorded with routine reversal of neuromuscular blockade using galantamine. Following therapeutic administration, delirium resolution was accompanied by restoration of meaningful interaction without sedatives. These retrospective observational findings support further investigation of prophylactic and therapeutic galantamine use. The observations of restored interaction prompted the hypothesis that galantamine could act as an agent promoting emergence from anesthesia.

after.authors: Dai, Y.; Guo, W.; Zhang, Y.; Yan, W.; Zheng, P.; Lian, Z.; Gu, G.; Wang, X.; Chen, X.; Wong, C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Cardiology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases, China
after.abstract: Background and Aims Chemokines regulate immune-cell trafficking, inflammation, and tissue repair in cardiovascular disease. C-C motif chemokine ligand 17 (CCL17) has been linked to adverse remodelling after myocardial infarction and neurohumoral stress, but its role during sustained mechanical pressure overload remains unclear. We investigated whether CCL17 regulates ventricular remodelling through signalling in cardiac fibroblasts. Methods We performed serum proteomic screening and assessed CCL17 in human serum and myocardial samples. We evaluated CCL17 function in mice subjected to transverse aortic constriction using global Ccl17 deletion and adeno-associated virus-mediated CCL17 augmentation. We used cardiac transcriptomics and pharmacological, small interfering RNA, and promoter-reporter experiments in cardiac fibroblasts to investigate downstream signalling. We tested the functional contribution of Igfbp6 in vivo using fibroblast-directed silencing. Results Serum CCL17 concentrations and myocardial CCL17 abundance were higher in patients with aortic stenosis than in controls. after.abstract: Background: Prolonged hospitalisation is an important burden among patients with sickle cell disease (SCD), with implications for healthcare utilisation and patient and caregiver burden. Early prediction may support timely clinical and resource-management interventions. Objective: To identify factors associated with prolonged hospitalisation among patients with SCD and compare the predictive performance of multivariable logistic regression with five supervised machine-learning algorithms. Methods: This retrospective study included SCD inpatients aged [≥]16 years admitted to the University of Ghana Hospital between January 2019 and December 2024. Logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, support vector machine, and k-nearest neighbours models were developed using five-fold stratified cross-validation. Class weighting and SMOTE were applied within training folds. Model performance was evaluated using AUC-ROC, AUC-PR, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), F1 score, and balanced accuracy. Results: Among 872 patients, 137 (15.7%) experienced prolonged hospitalisation. Acute chest syndrome (aOR=4.28; 95% CI: 2.31-7.94), malaria (aOR=3.77; 95% CI: 2.11-6.74), pneumonia (aOR=3.45; 95% CI: 2.02-5.90), and anaemia (aOR=2.71; 95% CI: 1.13-6.51) were independently associated with prolonged hospitalisation, whereas higher haemoglobin was protective (aOR=0.86; 95% CI: 0.78-0.96). Logistic regression achieved the highest AUC-ROC (0.692), F1 score (0.418) and balanced accuracy (0.677), while random forest achieved the highest AUC-PR (0.375). KNN had the highest sensitivity (59.3%) and XGBoost the highest specificity (87.2%). AUC-ROC confidence intervals overlapped substantially across models. Conclusion: Infection-related complications and anaemia were important predictors of prolonged hospitalisation, while higher haemoglobin was protective. ML models showed modest performance without clear superiority over logistic regression. Larger multicentre studies with external validation are warranted.

after.authors: Rao, U.; Pawar, R.; Beri, A.; Chadha, S.; Vashistha, H.; Das, M.
after.abstract: BACKGROUND: Active case finding (ACF) in India screens large populations to find few cases. AI-NETRA predicts neighbourhood-level tuberculosis (TB) risk from routine notification data and generates field microplans. OBJECTIVE: To compare the yield and efficiency of AI-guided and standard ACF, and frontline acceptability. DESIGN: Prospective quasi-experimental evaluation in four TB Units of Pune district, comparing two-week AI-guided sweeps (April to May 2026) with the routine campaign in the same units (December 2024 to January 2025). Primary endpoint: bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB per persons screened; secondary: all-forms yield, presumptive yield, referral precision, number needed to screen (NNS) and cost per case. Acceptability: 16 focus groups (n=100) and a survey of 101 ASHAs. RESULTS: AI-guided teams screened 66,095 people and confirmed 10 pulmonary cases, against 9 among 177,322 in the standard campaign (rate ratio 2.98, 95% CI 1.09 to 8.29); NNS was 6,610 versus 19,702 and cost per case 66% lower. All-forms detection did not differ (15 versus 32; RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.39); the standard campaign had mobile X-ray. 96% of ASHAs reported finding the same presumptive cases while screening fewer people. CONCLUSION: Geospatial targeting raised confirmed yield per person and lowered NNS; total detection did not differ. A concurrent, like-for-like trial is warranted.

after.title: Preprint: Individualized systems-informed corrective exercise for adults meeting prespecified criteria for upper crossed syndrome: protocol for a randomized controlled trial
after.authors: Khorami Moghadam, M.; Ghasemi, G. A.; PoorSaadat, L.; Golpayegani, M.
after.abstract: Background: Heterogeneity in eligibility criteria, intervention content, and exercise-progression rules has limited the reproducibility of research on upper crossed syndrome. This trial will examine the added effect of a structured, individualized, staged corrective-exercise program on adults who meet prespecified criteria for this phenotype. Methods: In this parallel randomized controlled trial, 36 women and men aged 18-40 years with forward head and shoulder posture and increased thoracic kyphosis will be allocated 1:1, stratified by sex. Over 12 weeks, both groups will attend three sessions per week and receive stationary cycling, indication-based stretching and mobilization, and education on healthy movement habits. The intervention group will additionally receive a systems-informed program encompassing restoration of range of motion, muscle-activation retraining, correction of movement patterns, progressive load tolerance, and preparation for health-enhancing physical activity. The primary outcome is the baseline-adjusted week-12 between-group difference in a multivariate profile comprising the forward-head, forward-shoulder, and thoracic-kyphosis angles. Scapular-muscle electromyography, range of motion, and balance are secondary outcomes. The primary exploratory electroencephalographic outcome is change in central relative alpha power during quiet standing with eyes open. Posture, range of motion, and balance will be assessed at baseline, week 12, and four-week follow-up; electromyography and electroencephalography at baseline and week 12. The primary analysis will use MANCOVA adjusted for baseline and sex, with Pillai's trace; longitudinal analyses will use linear mixed models. Effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals will be reported. Conclusions: This study will test the added effect of a reproducible corrective-exercise framework beyond the shared active-control components. The four-week follow-up will not support inference about long-term prevention of recurrence. Ethics and trial registration: Ethics approval: IR.UI.REC.1404.053. Trial registration: IRCT20250921067305N1.

after.authors: Jaraj, D.; Andren, K.; Hellstrom, P.; Laurell, K.; Zetterberg, H.; Wikkelso, C.; Tullberg, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Hydrocephalus Research Unit, Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Institute of Neuroscience and Physiology, The Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg, S
after.abstract: Background The underlying pathophysiology of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is incompletely understood and reliable predictors of shunt response are lacking. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers may provide insights into disease mechanisms and help identify patients most likely to benefit from surgery. The aim of this study was to explore CSF biomarker dynamics following shunt surgery and their relationship with clinical outcome. Methods The POiNT (Prediction of Outcome in iNPH) was a prospective longitudinal study. One hundred and thirty-five patients with iNPH underwent standardized clinical assessment and lumbar CSF sampling 3.6 (SD 2.1) months before and 5.7 months (SD 2.4) after shunt surgery. CSF was analyzed for biomarkers of astrogliosis, axonal injury, amyloid, and tau pathology, and synaptic dysfunction. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the iNPH scale. Associations between baseline biomarker levels, postoperative biomarker changes, and clinical outcomes were evaluated using adjusted correlation and regression analyses. Results In total, 69% (n=93) improved after shunt surgery. Substantial postoperative increases were observed for most CSF biomarkers: The largest relative increases were seen for growth-associated protein 43 (GAP43) (2.92-fold change), followed by Phosphorylated tau (2.65-fold change), Neurogranin and total-tau (both 2.29-fold change) as well as A{beta}40 (1.93-fold change), and A{beta}42 (1.76-fold change) (all p<0.001). In adjusted analyses, postoperative change in several biomarker levels were associated with degree of clinical improvement. However, baseline biomarker levels generally showed limited predictive value. Lower baseline monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP1) levels were associated with greater odds of overall clinical improvement but had a modest predictive performance (AUC 0.67). No baseline biomarker demonstrated strong discrimination of treatment response. Conclusion Shunt surgery was associated with substantial changes in CSF biomarker concentrations, several of which correlated with the degree of clinical improvement. Although baseline levels did not predict clinical outcome, the observed biomarker changes may reflect biological responses to treatment, altered CSF dynamics, or both .iNPH. Future studies examining these processes relating to disease reversibility might help elucidate pathophysiological mechanisms in iNPH.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Public Health Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, South Korea
after.abstract: Environmental chemical exposures may influence biological aging, but their relationships with epigenetic aging and related health outcomes remain incompletely understood. In this study, we evaluated the associations of 13 environmental exposures, including heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), with epigenetic aging in 666 older adults from the Forensic Research via Omics Markers in Environmental Health Vulnerable Areas (FROM) cohort. Among the evaluated epigenetic aging biomarkers, GrimAge acceleration showed the most prominent associations, with 2-hydroxyfluorene (2-HF), 2-naphthol (2-NAP), blood cadmium (bCd), and methylhippuric acid (MHA) exhibiting significant positive associations (strongest for 2-HF: beta = 0.491 years per doubling of exposure, P = 1.22 x 10-14). Quantile g-computation showed that combined environmental exposures were significantly associated with increased GrimAge acceleration (psi = 0.497, 95% CI: 0.013-0.981, P = 0.044), and Bayesian kernel machine regression identified 2-HF and 2-NAP as major contributors. Among clinical traits, white blood cell count (WBC) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) were significantly and positively associated with GrimAge acceleration, and two-sample Mendelian randomization provided nominal support for a positive effect of GrimAge acceleration on GGT. Mediation analyses identified significant indirect effects through GrimAge acceleration for the associations of 2-HF, 2-NAP, bCd, and MHA with GGT. Exploratory disease analyses further suggested potential associations with diabetic nephropathy and osteoporosis, together with an inverse association with cardiac valvular disease. These findings suggest that environmental chemical exposures are associated with accelerated epigenetic aging, which may represent a biological pathway linking environmental exposures to metabolic and age-related health outcomes.

after.authors: Raper, A. C.; Schultz, B. I.; Kim, J.; Wubbenhorst, B. S.; Martin, A.; Rohanizadegan, M.; Hartman, T. R.; Cohen, S.; Chai, T.; Dagar, A.; Haley, J.; Li, J.; Carey, D.; Regeneron Genetics Center,  ; Penn Medicine Biobank,  ; Hockemeyer, D.; Stewart, D. R.; Nathanson, K. L.
after.abstract: Background: The prevalence of germline POT1 variants, spectrum of associated tumors, cancer risk and survival outcomes are incompletely described, and clinical management guidelines vary. We evaluated POT1 variant carriers in three biobanks and a clinical cohort to address these limitations. Methods: Prevalence, cancer spectrum and risk associated with germline POT1 pathogenic/likely pathogenic and additional functionally assessed variants were evaluated in Penn Medicine Biobank (PMBB; n=51,172), Geisinger MyCode (MyCode; n=220,582), UK Biobank (UKBB; n=469,558) and a Penn Medicine clinical cohort. Results: Estimated POT1 variant prevalence ranged from 1:1,279 to 1:2,902. Compared to non-carriers, cancer diagnoses were more frequent among POT1 variant carriers in PMBB (OR 3.41, 95%CI 1.81-6.43, p=1.88x10-4), MyCode (OR 2.23, 95%CI 1.31-3.79, p=0.003), and UKBB (OR 1.40, 95%CI 1.07-1.84, p=0.015). Cancer incidence increased beginning in the mid-30s, without evidence of increased mortality. Along with previously described cancer types, lung cancer was associated with POT1 variant carriers in two biobank cohorts. Conclusion: POT1 is a cancer susceptibility gene associated with a moderate (1.5-3.5-fold) increased cancer risk. Variants are relatively frequent and predispose to a broad tumor spectrum and increased incidence starting in the mid-30s, without increasing mortality. These findings expand understanding of POT1-associated disease and provide data to inform clinical management.

Variants are relatively frequent and predispose to a broad tumor spectrum and increased incidence starting in the mid-30s, without increasing mortality. These findings expand understanding of POT1-associated disease and provide data to inform clinical management.

after.abstract: Background: Functional disability, malnutrition, and psychological well-being in older people are deeply interconnected. A better understanding of these conditions is crucial for geriatric care. This study aims to assess the status of functional disability, malnutrition status, and psychological well-being among older people. Methods: Participants were assessed for disability in activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL), malnutrition by Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA) tool, and psychological well-being was evaluated by the WHO-5 Well-Being Index. A multistage cluster sampling probability proportionate to size method was used for sampling, and 360 people aged 60 years and older were selected from the Lalitpur district of Nepal. Data on socio-demographic factors, functional ability, malnutrition, and psychological well-being were collected. Statistical analysis was performed including bivariate analysis to compare genders. Results: The functional disability rate according to ADL was 34.7%, and with IADL disability, it was 47.8%, with higher in women as compared to men. According to the MNA score, this study found a 13% prevalence of malnutrition and 45% at risk of malnutrition. In the WHO well-being index score, 32.8% had a score of < 13, reflecting poor psychological well-being. Conclusion: Nearly one-third of the participants were dependent on ADL, reflecting a high disability rate. About half of the population had poor nutritional status, and nearly one-third of the study sample was experiencing poor psychological well-being. This study findings demonstrate the importance of managing problems with appropriate screening, rehabilitation, and therapeutic measures for the physical and psychological well-being of older people in the community. Key words: Malnutrition, Disability, Well being index, Older people, Nepal

after.title: Preprint: Network scaling in swarm learning across real hospitals of different sizes: a KPI-driven analysis on the eICU Collaborative Research Database
after.authors: Gebremariam, D.; Mantovani, M.; Combi, C.
after.abstract: Background. Distributed learning lets hospitals train prediction models jointly without exchanging patient records, but how the benefits of a swarm network change as it grows, and which hospitals gain most, have so far been studied with artificial partitions of single-center databases. We examined network scaling on real hospitals that differ in size, volume and sepsis prevalence. Methods. We applied the seven-KPI swarm-learning evaluation framework (Swarm Gain, Local Gain, Relative Local Gain, Model Stability Index, Jain's index, Data Utility Index and label entropy) to progressive network scaling on the eICU Collaborative Research Database. From 25 hospitals (71,887 ICU stays; sepsis prevalence 16.6%), six hospitals stratified by bed size (two small, two medium, two large; 14,776 stays) formed networks of two, four and six hospitals in all six category-joining orders; four further hospitals served as substitutes in robustness checks. Swarm learning was simulated with the client-controlled workflow of NVIDIA FLARE (federated averaging, 30 rounds, five random seeds). The task was whole-stay sepsis classification from discretized vital-sign, laboratory and medication features with a 1,313-parameter feedforward network, with AUROC as the metric. Results. Network AUROC increased with every addition in every ordering, from 0.734 (small-first), 0.755 (medium-first) and 0.781 (large-first) at two hospitals to 0.804 (SD 0.002) at six. Swarm Gain exceeded 1 at all nine unique transitions (mean 1.042 for two-to-four and 1.020 for four-to-six hospitals). Every hospital had Local Gain below 1; relative improvement over local training ranged from 4.1% for the strongest hospital (local AUROC 0.773) to 29.5% for the weakest (0.621), averaging 25.5% for small and 5.9% for large hospitals. Adding large hospitals gave existing members the largest gain (mean Relative Local Gain +6.2%); adding small hospitals never reduced it. Seed-to-seed variability fell from a coefficient of variation of 2.2% at two hospitals to 0.2% at six. Feature distributions were near-identical across hospitals (Data Utility Index 0.005-0.013), whereas the change in label entropy tracked Swarm Gain (r = 0.74). Substituting alternative medium or large hospitals left network AUROC between 0.790 and 0.805. Conclusions. On real multi-hospital data, swarm participation improved every hospital's model, most for hospitals with the weakest local models, with no transition in which an addition harmed the network. Because all orderings end in the same six-hospital network, joining order affected only intermediate performance. The results characterize the KPI framework under real inter-hospital variation in volume and label prevalence and support inclusive recruitment anchored by large hospitals. Per-hospital evaluation and warm-started sequential joining are needed to quantify member-level effects.

after.authors: Judson, S.; Pennington, J.; Haring, C.; Stephan, N.; Yuson, M.; Lee, S.; Kenu, E.; Dowdy, D.
after.abstract: Background: Multiple recent yellow fever (YF) outbreaks have occurred despite a highly effective vaccine. Increasing vaccination coverage and decreasing response times have been key components of the Eliminate Yellow Fever Epidemics (EYE) strategy. However, the combined impacts of these factors on YF outbreaks, especially since implementation of the EYE strategy in 2017, remain uncertain. Methods: We developed mathematical models to simulate the effects of vaccination coverage and timing, calibrating them to recent YF outbreaks in Ghana (2021-2022) and South Sudan (2023-2024). We then projected YF morbidity and mortality under different EYE strategy thresholds for vaccination coverage and timing. Results: In Ghana, where reactive vaccination was observed at 22 days with an estimated 70% baseline coverage, modeled delays of 60 and 120 days yielded 62 (95% uncertainty interval [UI] 30-119) and 281 (95% UI 59-927) additional severe cases, respectively. Increasing baseline vaccination coverage to 80% averted an estimated 20 severe cases (95% UI 14-25). In South Sudan, where reactive vaccination occurred at 61 days with estimated 50% baseline coverage, shortening the response time to 20 days and increasing baseline coverage to 80% averted an estimated 80 (95% UI 68-91) and 95 severe cases (95% UI 80-112) independently or 103 severe cases (95% UI 85-120) if combined. Conclusion: Increasing baseline YF vaccination coverage to at least 80% can avert substantial morbidity from YF outbreaks. Decreasing vaccination response time for reactive vaccination can provide additional benefit.

after.authors: Wamalwa, P. N.; Mugo, C.; Ngaruiya, C.
after.abstract: **Abstract** **Background** Young adults with type 1 diabetes (T1D) in low- and middle-income countries experience persistently poor glycaemic control despite improved insulin access. Evidence on the effects of social determinants of health (SDOH) on glycaemic control, complications, and psychological well-being remains limited, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. We examined relationships between SDOH, psychological health, glycaemic control, and early complication markers among young adults with T1D in Kenya. **Methods** We conducted a multicentre cross-sectional study among 164 adults aged 18-34 years attending four diabetes clinics in Kenya. SDOH were assessed using a prespecified, context-informed questionnaire covering six domains. Psychological well-being was assessed using PAID, PHQ-9, and GAD-7. Clinical outcomes included HbA1c, a single urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), and lipid profile. Associations between SDOH domains and clinical and psychological outcomes were evaluated using multivariable ordinal and binary logistic regression models adjusted for age, sex, and diabetes duration. **Findings** Mean age was 24.96+/-4.35 years and diabetes duration 7.26+/-5.70 years. Mean HbA1c was 11.5+/-3.44%, with only 4.9% achieving <7%. LDL cholesterol was above target in 56.1%, 64.0% had an elevated LDL/HDL ratio, and 28.0% had elevated UACR. Diabetes distress and clinically significant depressive symptoms affected 30.5% and 27.5%, respectively. Moderate-to-high SDOH burden was greatest for economic stability (76.8%), social/community context (52.4%), and food environment (43.9%). All SDOH domains showed positive but non-significant associations with HbA1c. Diabetes distress was associated with economic instability (aOR 1.42, 95% CI 1.17-1.72), healthcare system burden (1.45, 1.12-1.87), neighbourhood/physical environment burden (1.39, 1.07-1.80), and food environment burden (1.30, 1.03-1.64). Anxiety was associated with social/community (1.70, 1.14-2.53) and healthcare system burden (1.68, 1.19-2.36). Economic instability was associated with elevated UACR (1.40, 1.05-1.85). **Discussion** Young adults with T1D in Kenya experience substantial social and psychological burden alongside poor glycaemic control and early complication markers. Social disadvantage appears to influence kidney disease complications, and psychological well-being regardless of glycaemic control in our sample, underscoring the need to move beyond glucose-centered care. Poor glycaemic control was pervasive, which likely obviated any detectable differences by SDOH in this population. Ultimately, Integrated care addressing SDOH and mental health may support more sustainable long-term outcomes. Key words: Type 1 diabetes; Social determinants; glycemic control; complications, psychological health

after.authors: Gomez, A. M.; Olarte Escobar, N. M.; Valderrama Marquez, I. A.; Castellanos Corredor, J. E.; Lopez Cruz, R. L.; Escobar, J.; Rico Mendoza, A.; Porras Ramirez, A.
after.abstract: Background Congenital syphilis remains a preventable cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, and its incidence in Colombia remains well above the elimination target. We aimed to identify maternal and prenatal care factors associated with congenital syphilis among women with gestational syphilis attended in a public health network serving socially vulnerable populations in Bogota, Colombia. Methods We conducted a retrospective case-control study using surveillance and clinical records from the Subred Integrada de Servicios de Salud Sur E.S.E. for pregnancies ending between 2017 and 2024. Cases were neonates with congenital syphilis according to national surveillance criteria; controls were neonates without congenital syphilis born to mothers with gestational syphilis in the same network. Factors associated with congenital syphilis were identified using multivariable logistic regression with backward elimination. Results We included 743 mother-infant pairs (285 cases and 458 controls). Maternal diagnosis after 28 weeks of gestation (adjusted odds ratio 17.75; 95% confidence interval 11.81-26.69), absence of prenatal care compared with eight or more visits (12.74; 5.03-32.25) and reinfection during pregnancy (3.02; 1.73-5.29) were independently associated with congenital syphilis, whereas a documented history of syphilis was associated with lower odds (0.45; 0.25-0.82). The model showed high discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.860). Migrant status was associated with congenital syphilis in the crude analysis but not after adjustment. Conclusions Congenital syphilis in this setting was associated mainly with late maternal diagnosis and absent prenatal care, conditions that preclude timely benzathine penicillin treatment. Strengthening early prenatal screening, continuity of care and partner management may reduce vertical transmission in socially vulnerable urban populations.

after.authors: Perez-Saez, J.; Lee, E. C.; Zheng, Q.; Kamadjeu, R.; Zaitchik, B. F.; Azman, A. S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Global Health, University of Geneva
after.abstract: Cholera is considered a paradigm for climate-sensitive diseases, yet its relation with El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the dominant mode of interannual climate variability, remains poorly quantified in Africa where most cholera deaths occur. Using 15 years of surveillance data across 30 African countries and novel statistical and simulation frameworks, we identify five geographically coherent ENSO-cholera teleconnection groups, each characterized by distinct directions, strengths and timing of effects on outbreak occurrence, duration and incidence. For the unfolding major El Nino of 2026-27, we project two- to five-fold greater cholera burden in Eastern and Horn of Africa than under ENSO-neutral conditions. These findings identify immediate priorities for anticipatory action and establish a dynamic framework for attributing burden for outbreak-prone diseases to climate variability.

after.abstract: Objective: To describe global patterns of resting heart rate (RHR) in population subgroups and over time. Methods: Observational data from WHO STEP surveys (n=363,462 participants from 76 countries, 2002-2020) and the South Asia Biobank (SAB, n=203,524 participants from four South Asian countries, 2018-2023). RHR was measured in triplicate while seated using a blood pressure cuff. Height and weight were measured using anthropometric techniques. Physical activity was self-reported and accelerometry-measured (SAB subsample, n=22,183). We describe RHR distributions by geographical region, temporality, sex, age, BMI, and physical activity. Utility of RHR to explain accelerometer-based physical activity was examined by regression. Results: Country-level median RHR ranged 65-80 bpm, higher in women than men. Age-related RHR patterns diverged markedly by sex; men showing a curvilinear association with higher RHR in midlife, and women showing a consistent decline with age across most regions. after.title: Preprint: Community Care of Eating Disorders: Comparison of Online and In-Person Treatment. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
after.authors: Hamid, N.; Robinson, P.
after.abstract: Objective: Eating disorders are serious conditions which sometimes require intensive treatment and are undertreated worldwide. Care can be provided in the community in different treatment delivery modes that could increase access to evidence-based treatment and avoid the negative impacts of delayed interventions. This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated the comparative effectiveness of adult eating disorder community care delivered via in-person, online and mixed (blended/hybrid) modes to provide a global perspective and recommendations for the use of telemedicine in the field. Method: The databases MEDLINE, Embase, PsychINFO, Emcare, Scopus and Web of Science were searched on 22nd June 2025. Inclusion criteria specified quasi-experimental studies which compared two or more treatment delivery modes. The Joanna Briggs Institute risk of bias tool for quasi-experimental studies was used for quality assessments. Qualitative synthesis and meta-analyses were conducted. Results: The daycare/intensive outpatient programme studies showed non-inferiority of in-person and online treatment programmes: EDE-Q Global score (-0.00 [95% CI: -0.23, 0.22]); anxiety (GAD-7/OASIS) (-0.05 [95% CI: -0.31, 0.20]); BMI (0.06 [95% CI: -0.20, 0.33]); and depression (BDI-2/PHQ-9/CES-D) (0.07 [95% CI: -0.31, 0.44]). The outpatient studies showed non-significant differences between in-person and online treatment programmes: anxiety (GAD-7/PROMIS) (0.28 [95% CI: -0.48, 1.04]); depression (PHQ-9/PROMIS) (0.58 [95% CI: -0.59, 1.75]); and EDE-Q Global score (0.73 [95% CI: -0.91, 2.36]). For all measures, better outcomes were indicated for online care. Discussion: Comparisons with mixed treatment delivery mode are lacking, but findings provide credence to the viability of online care as being on par or even better under certain conditions than in-person care.
